comparison: Both strongly agree on the contextualization of results within prior literature (C77-C88). OpenEval finds the comparison to prior work appropriate and well-cited, while peer reviewers explicitly accept the positioning relative to Clark et al. (2012) and other studies. Both view the synthesis as reinforcing existing paradigms.

Both support the initial comparative analysis between complexes and pathways (C39-C48). OpenEval validates the statistical tests and interpretation that co-functionality confounds physical interaction contributions. Peer reviewers accept these descriptive findings without question, with Reviewer 1 stating 'various analyses nicely support the authors' claims.'

Both support the computational methodology and statistical procedures (C36-C38, C93-C97). OpenEval finds the Fisher transformation and Winsorization appropriate and well-justified. Peer reviewers do not question the analytical approach, with acceptance implicit in their praise for the 'compelling' evidence and 'smart experimental design.'

Divergence in evaluation type: OpenEval rates the hypothesis about nonphysical forces (C8, C89-C92) as UNCERTAIN, noting it remains speculative and requires additional experiments. Peer reviewers rate it as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 stating it 'reinforces the existing paradigm that covariation is driven by a varied/mixed set of interaction-types.'

Both strongly support the study design and dataset (C26-C28, C31-C35, C49-C51, C69-C70). OpenEval validates the methodology as sound with appropriate sample sizes. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the approach, with Reviewer 1 noting it's 'better positioned' than previous work and Reviewer 2 calling it 'very smart experimental design.'

Both support the proportional rank analysis findings (C61-C65). OpenEval validates the permutation tests and interpretation that most complexes lack significant physical interaction signal. Peer reviewers accept these heterogeneous results, with Reviewer 2 acknowledging the 'nuanced and sometimes inconclusive results' and expressing satisfaction with the authors' language.

Both support the ROC analysis and global permutation test results (C52-C60, C72-C75). OpenEval validates the statistical tests and notes the p=0.08 appropriately fails significance. Peer reviewers accept these mixed results, with the editor's statement about 'difficult to quantify' contributions aligning with the nuanced statistical findings.

Both strongly support the main conclusions (C5-C7, C29-C30, C66-C68, C71-C76). OpenEval finds the 'weak but present' conclusion appropriately nuanced and supported by multiple lines of evidence. All three peer reviewers affirm the conclusions without challenge, with the editor describing 'compelling evidence' and reviewers noting the analyses 'nicely support the authors' claims.'

Both support the foundational ERC concepts and background (C1-C3, C9-C12). OpenEval validates these as well-supported by established literature. Peer reviewers implicitly accept the framework through their descriptions of the study addressing 'covariation of evolutionary rates' without questioning any background claims or definitions.

Both support the characterization of prior literature and research gap (C4, C13-C15, C20-C25). OpenEval validates the identification of contradictory prior work as appropriately cited. Peer reviewers accept this contextualization without critique, implicitly through their acceptance of the study's motivation and positioning.

Both support the global permutation test results (C58-C60). OpenEval validates the p=0.08 as appropriately failing significance and providing important context. Peer reviewers accept this nuanced finding as part of the evidence that physical interaction contributions are 'difficult to quantify.'

Both support the SMC5-SMC6 example (C16-C19). OpenEval validates this as an effective illustration of the ERC concept with appropriate interpretation. Peer reviewers do not question this example, accepting it as part of the foundational framework without raising concerns.

Both support the methodological advantages claims (C69-C70). OpenEval validates the 343 species providing more power and finds the domain-level rationale reasonable. Peer reviewers explicitly praise this aspect, with Reviewer 1 noting the study is 'better positioned' with more species and Reviewer 2 praising the domain-level resolution.
